A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same work with the same title and authors. The complete main texts, figures, tables, equations and appendices are readable, and retained material can be matched across relocation and renumbering.

before.justification: v1 reports original synthetic experiments, sensitivity and sample-size analyses, and an International Stroke Trial policy-learning experiment.

after.justification: v2 retains original experiments and additionally reports an IHDP benchmark and synthetic experiments with increasing numbers of treatment options.

M1.justification: The sharp-bound formulas, one-step estimator, regret extension, nuisance components and policy updates are retained. v2 mentions optional cross-fitting but explicitly retains the single-split Algorithm 1; the added explanation does not establish a changed estimator or learning procedure.

E1.justification: Appendix D adds IHDP, covering home-visit decisions and infant cognitive outcomes. Appendix C extends the binary synthetic experiments to scenarios with 2–10 actions. These expand the evaluated population and decision scenarios; the four-treatment stroke task already existed in v1.

E2.justification: v2 Figure 3 includes Kallus–Zhou across the sensitivity-misspecification sweep, whereas v1 Figure 2 omits it and the accompanying text quotes only its correctly specified result. Other comparator identities are retained, and IHDP uses the existing baseline set.

E3.justification: New protocols include varying action count while fixing true and specified confounding at Γ=5, and IHDP preprocessing that deletes 60% of specified low-covariate observations, hides three covariates and sweeps Γ from 1.0 to 2.3. The stroke plot also uses a revised sensitivity grid. Shared neural hyperparameters and the 0.5 sample split remain unchanged.

E4.justification: Appendix C adds a substantive stress test of performance as multiclass propensity estimation becomes harder. The misspecification analysis gains the Kallus–Zhou response curve, and the stroke analysis examines deterioration at small Γ. The existing sample-size comparison against the plug-in estimator is retained.

E5.justification: Both versions state that results are averaged over 10 seeds and report uncertainty through ± entries and graphical bars or bands. No changed run count, new uncertainty-estimation procedure or significance test is specified.

E6.justification: v2 adds IHDP results in Table 3 and action-space results in Figure 6. Existing plotted results also change: plug-in regret at 1,500 samples shifts from approximately −0.58 to −0.53. v2 Table 2 preserves v1 Table 1's even-Γ values but omits its odd-Γ columns, and the stroke results use a revised grid.

T1.justification: v2 replaces positivity with strong overlap and adds finite-moment and locally positive continuous-density assumptions to Theorem 4.3 and the appendix regret estimator. Appendix F.2 adds a canonical-gradient justification and explains where regularity assumptions enter the derivation. These refine the existing theory; estimator formulas and most proof steps remain unchanged.

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction and conclusion retain the claims of sharp value bounds, efficient estimation, avoidance of minimax optimization, learning guarantees and extension to policy improvement. Replacing 'statistically efficient' with 'semi-parametrically efficient' clarifies terminology without introducing a different central contribution.

C2.justification: Appendices B–C add detailed explanations linking Kallus–Zhou's global thresholding to propagated propensity errors and conservative reversion to the baseline. v2 distinguishes sharp regret bounds from sharp value bounds and qualifies the stroke robustness claim by explaining failure at small Γ through insufficient confounding protection and nuisance-estimation complexity.

D1.justification: Appendix G newly reports approximately 20 seconds of training for 1,000 synthetic samples on an AMD Ryzen 7 Pro CPU with 32 GB RAM. The new experiments provide additional preprocessing and control details. Existing network configurations, training hyperparameters, sample split and code-access information are retained.

R1.justification: v2 adds a related-methods table and a dedicated technical comparison with Kallus–Zhou, explicitly acknowledging sharpness for regret while distinguishing value bounds. It also expands positioning against mean-effect sensitivity methods, binary-treatment approaches, dynamic-policy methods and Rambachan et al.'s outcome sensitivity model, with corresponding new citations.

P1.justification: The main narrative and section sequence remain largely intact. v2 standardizes efficiency terminology, condenses the experimental subsections, expands selected explanations, removes the impact statement and inserts new appendices before the relocated sensitivity guidance, proofs and implementation details.

P2.justification: The main text changes from two columns to a single-column conference layout with extensively repositioned displays. v2 adds a conceptual figure, comparison table and experimental displays, reduces the original confounding table's columns, restyles the bar charts and replaces the stroke line plot with grouped bars.

improvement.justification: Explicit regularity conditions, fuller baseline comparisons and the action-space stress test improve rigor and empirical transparency. The gains are limited by reporting problems in the additions: IHDP's stated deletion rule is identical across treatment arms, leaving the claimed induction of confounding unclear, and Figure 5 peaks at Γ=22 although the text still identifies Γ=24.
